rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Tables 1-3; the authors run their own EPANET/Monte Carlo model (OPTIEN) of the Fuente Palmera network using 2007 telemetry demand data and report pressures, power and energy for four management scenarios.
rows.notes: The study's own results concern energy and power requirements of an on-demand pressurised network under alternative management (dynamic pressure head, sectoring), giving energy savings of up to ~27%. It reports no result of its own on conveyance efficiency, water losses or water conservation; the statements in the Introduction that conveyance efficiency rises from 60-70% to near 100% and that water consumption fell up to 50% are cited from Rodriguez Diaz et al. (2008), not measured here. Water consumption is held constant across scenarios by design. Simulation outputs were not compared with measured pressures/energy.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Tables 1-3; own simulation runs of the Fuente Palmera network with measured 2007 demand data.
rows.notes: The study does not test drip, micro or sprinkler irrigation at all; it simulates energy requirements of on-demand pressurised network management. The only mention of trickle/sprinklers is an introductory remark that pressurised networks allow farmers to use such on-farm systems, with no own data on drip water use or conservation. Technology in the passage (drip) differs from that studied (network management/pumping scenarios).

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a hydraulic/energy simulation of an irrigation district (scheme scale) focused on energy savings from pressure regulation and sectoring; it contains no own evidence on water conservation or on-farm irrigation methods, so both claim rows fail Q2.
